A numeral is converted where it stands, into the type that its place fixes,
and not before, because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect numerals to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it to a floating-point number before its place is known
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used where a floating-point interval is expected,
it is better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
In \library, each of the eight number types (\secref{basic-rationals}) declares
a coercion from \TYP{NaturalNumeral}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
and \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} declare one from \TYP{RadixPointNumeral}, each generic
over the four numbers, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} declares
\EXP{\KWD{coerce}\llbracket\KWD{nat} n,\KWD{nat} r,\KWD{nat} v\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket)}.
The parameter of such a coercion has no value: its body computes the type's
value from the four numbers, which it reads as values, integers of type
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\secref{natparams}).
The conversion is exact into the five integer types (\secref{basic-integers})
and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and rounds once, to the nearest value of the type, into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}.
At a numeral, the compiler instantiates the coercion at the numeral's four
numbers and evaluates it: a value that the Java Virtual Machine holds as an
\texttt{int}, a \texttt{long}, a \texttt{float} or a \texttt{double} is a
constant of the compiled code, and any other value, as one of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}
or \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, is made once for the place where the numeral stands, so
that every evaluation of that place yields the same value.

A place \emph{fixes a type} for a numeral when the type declared there declares
a coercion from the numeral's type, as each number type of \library\ does and a
type of a program's own may.
The declared type of a variable, a field or a parameter, and the declared
return type of a functional, are such places, the parameter types of the
declaration that a call invokes among them (\secref{resolving-coercion}).
There the numeral is converted into that type, from its exact value:
so \EXP{q\COLON\mathbb{Q} = 0.1} binds the rational \EXP{1/10},
\EXP{r\COLON\mathbb{R}64 = 0.1} the floating-point number nearest to it, and
\EXP{n\COLON\mathbb{N}32 = 5} the natural number 5.
It is a static error if the numeral's value lies outside the range of that
type, or rounds to an infinity there.
Where nothing fixes a type, as where a variable is declared without a type, or
a parameter has the type \TYP{Any}, \TYP{Object} or \TYP{Number} or a type
parameter declared without a bound, the numeral is converted into its
\emph{default}: a numeral without a radix point into \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or into
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value does not fit in the
narrower type, and a numeral with a radix point into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
So \EXP{x = 3} binds \VAR{x} as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
\EXP{\VAR{bigN} = 3000000000} binds \VAR{bigN} as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{y = 0.5} binds \VAR{y} as an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64};
\EXP{x \sequiv z} is \VAR{true} for \EXP{z\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = 3};
and for \EXP{\KWD{object}\;\TYP{Cell}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)},
\EXP{\TYP{Cell}(3)} is a \EXP{\TYP{Cell}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket}.
\secref{numeral-default} says where else a numeral takes its default, as where
several numerals fix one type parameter, and how a numeral whose conversions
tie is read.
The default applies to a numeral, and to a static expression of numerals once
it is folded (\secref{static-expr}), never to an expression of a numeral type.

A type of a program's own receives a numeral as the number types of \library\
do, through its own coercion from the numeral's type, generic over the four

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{literals}; \secref{coercion}.
\item[Change] \secref{literals} says that \library\ give every numeral without a
radix point the type \TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the
number types, and that each of the five integer types, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a coercion from it.
The box of \secref{coercion} says the same of the coercion into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, and that the interpreter does not yet give a numeral that
type.
The change of \secref{revival-numerals}, of 8 and 9~November 2026, replaced
this text: an integer numeral has the type
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}, beside
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket} for a numeral with a
radix point, types that exist only when a program is compiled and whose static
arguments are the numeral's four numbers, and it is converted into its default
where nothing fixes a type; this entry keeps the change of 29~September 2026,
and its effect below states what of it holds since then.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
....
\item[Effect] The type \TYP{IntLiteral} of this change is replaced, in
\library\ and in the compiled path's own library, by
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}, of which no value exists
when a program runs, since the change of \secref{revival-numerals}.
The compiled type checker converts an integer numeral to the
integer type, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} or \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} that its context expects,
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} among them, which refused a numeral
before.
A numeral beside a value of an integer type is converted to that type where no
declaration of the operator is applicable to the two without coercion, and that
type's own declaration of the operator is then the most specific
(\secref{resolving-coercion}); \library\ state on each integer type the
comparisons \EXP{<}, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{>} and \EXP{\geq}, \OPR{CMP},
\OPR{MAXNUM} and \OPR{MINNUM}, which the types inherited before from a
declaration that a converted numeral leaves tied with those of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
They stated a power with a numeral exponent too, which the change of
\secref{revival-numerals} removes: a numeral exponent reaches the power's
declarations over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \TYP{AnyIntegral}.
Equality was stated in pairs instead, each integer type declaring an \EXP{=}
whose parameter was of the numeral type, and the numeral type one whose
parameter was of each integer type; since the change of
\secref{revival-numerals} no such pair exists, no value of a numeral type
existing when a program runs (\secref{basic-rationals}).
Inequality was not stated in pairs: the top-level declaration of \EXP{\neq},
whose parameters are of type \TYP{Any}, is applicable to an integer value and a
numeral without coercion, and since the change of \secref{revival-numerals} it
receives the numeral at its default, which it compares with the integer value by
\EXP{=}; so on the interpreter \EXP{u \neq 0} is \VAR{true} for a zero \VAR{u}
of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} or \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, neither of which declares \EXP{=}
with \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and \EXP{u = 0} is \VAR{false}, as the effect of
\secref{revival-numerals} says with its rows.
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} states in its api, for the same reason, the additive and
multiplicative operators its body declares.
\TYP{IntLiteral} declared its own \VAR{zero}, \VAR{one}, \VAR{even},
\VAR{odd}, \VAR{floor}, \VAR{ceiling}, \VAR{truncate}, \OPR{DIVIDES},
\OPR{TIMES} and a power with a numeral exponent; \TYP{NaturalNumeral} declares
none of them, nor any other method, since an expression of numerals alone is
folded and a numeral reaches those of its default type
(\secref{revival-numerals}).
A numeral given where any integer type is accepted, as the count of a shift,
is converted to the narrowest of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} that holds its value, as \secref{numeral-default} reads a
numeral whose conversions tie.
The interpreter converts an integer numeral where its place fixes a type, and
gives it its default elsewhere (\secref{revival-numerals}).
Its calls of the comparisons, \OPR{CMP}, \OPR{MAXNUM} and \OPR{MINNUM} on an
integer type reach that type's own declarations, which answer as the
declarations inherited before did, except that \OPR{MAXNUM} and \OPR{MINNUM}
with a converted argument, which stopped at a tie with those of
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} or answered at \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, now answer at the integer
type both arguments convert to.

\seclabel{revival-asfloat}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{basic-rationals}; \secref{revival-numbers}.
\item[Change] The passage on the conversions between number types says that
the explicit conversion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x)}, is the
method that each number type declares, and that \TYP{Number} itself declares
no conversion, where it said that \library\ declare the method on
\TYP{Number}.
The change of \secref{revival-numbers} says the same.
\item[Rationale] The revival decided on 6~November 2026 that \VAR{asFloat}, and
the \EXP{=} that the library built on it, leave the trait \TYP{Number}, and that
each of the library's number types keeps its own \VAR{asFloat}.
The team's later compiler library declares \TYP{Number} with nothing in it
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss}, lines
510--511, in the revival's repository), and declares its conversion into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} on each of its number types, not on a shared trait; the
Working Draft names no such method.
With \TYP{Number} open to a program's own number types, an abstract
\VAR{asFloat} would oblige a program's complex number to give a float, and an
\EXP{=} on \TYP{Number} built on it would call two different complex numbers
equal.
\Library\ now declare \VAR{asFloat} on \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}
(\nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi};
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi}), and the vector
norm at each of the eight number types as its element type.
The revival decided on 9~November 2026 that the numeral types declare none,
since no value of a numeral type exists when a program runs
(\secref{revival-numerals}).
A reversal would declare \VAR{asFloat} on \TYP{Number} again, abstract, with an
\EXP{=} built on it, so that every type below \TYP{Number} must give a float, or
declare it on a new trait that the number types extend.
\item[Effect] \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x)} is unchanged at every number type of the
library.
Two numbers of different types compare by \EXP{=} where a coercion carries one
into the other: for each of the library's fourteen coercions between number
types, the type converted to declares \EXP{=} at the type converted from, and
that type declares \EXP{=} at the first, each converting the narrower operand as
the coercion does.
The library's eleven coercions from the two numeral types have no such pairs,
since no value of a numeral type exists when a program runs
(\secref{revival-numerals}).
Two numbers of different types that no coercion joins, as a \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}
and an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, compare by the library's fallback \EXP{=} over
\TYP{Any}, which answers \EXP{a \sequiv b}; a program that means their values
writes the conversion, \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x) = y}.
Two values of different types are never strictly equivalent
(\secref{equivalence}), so that fallback answers \VAR{false} for them, on the
interpreter as in the compiled code's helper.
A number type of a program's own compares by the \EXP{=} it declares, or else by
the fallback.
\item[Original text] The Working Draft of February 2011 has no such sentence:
the revival added it in its own text of 27~September 2026, not the Working
Draft's.

## 5. His words that carry each point

- 12:36 (L3260), on float numerals: "whatever ends up in QQ doesn't lose this precision. Whenever we know that we are saving the literal into float with fixed size, we should do the relevant conversion with maximum precision."
- 20:11 (L4329): "float literal is basically a QQ with implicit coercions to all other numerics. ... How could we get the promise of the conversion? Like, maybe we should try it on our own numeric types. What if we tried it with complex numbers? ... how would we try to stress test this concept of literal during a conversion like this so that we arrive at the right shape?"
- 20:18 (L4350): "didn't you just quote the solution from the specification with Radix point numeral? Like, I am seeing this for the first time here. Isn't the solution to implement this? I haven't seen it in walk, and we haven't seen it in compile path."
- 20:23 (L4361): "the specification was saying that you go for the conversion, that this conversion happens at compile time. We would never instantiate so many types at runtime, right? It is a compile time type. It doesn't exist at runtime."
- 20:29 (L4423): "the specification promises that the radix point numeral is a compile time conversion. It can only live on the right side of an assignment or declaration, and the left side must be a different type. You will never get radix point numeral or natural numeral at runtime."
- 21:22 (L4640): "We have the literals defined using this radix type. Like, we finished the design as the specification says. Does that solve all of our problems here? Do we need to prototype something to make this running?"
- 21:34 (L4676): "You never write int literal and float literal with the generic parameters N, M, R, and V. ... Value is the last of these generic parameters. It's the V at the end. ... how would you access those numbers inside the float literal? ... show me the code. ... use the same example that they use, those intervals. Show me the old way and the new way."
- 21:38 (L4689): "why can't we change the nat to be ZZ? Like a arbitrary precision integer, basically a big int. We are putting it into the type, so it must have a fixed size so that we can stamp the class. Is that the reason?"
- 21:40 (L4700): "this thing is supposed to be a compile time thing only. ... these are not runtime things. Why can't we accept for these types in a checker arbitrary precision size for the value?"
- 21:55 (L4749): "NAT, N-A-T, is just a natural number in generic type system with no limits. We have, for practical purposes, implemented it for the compile path as something that is ZZ32 ... But NAT is just a number that can be used in compilers' computations. ... Why can't we build it the specifications way? Just finish the original design. Why not? This way there is no runtime type that you are calling methods on that is not the compile time way, right? Using just the type system declaration for the coercion seems more elegant to me. The original drafts way."
- 22:02 (L4813): "how do I convert a numeral, a constant written in the program's name, into an instance of a custom numeric type? And you do it by letting the parser give you the four numbers, and you put them into the object's during compile time to compute its fields, so that you can stamp that object as a compile time constant."
- 22:14 (L4823): "you are saying the compiler runs coerce only at runtime. It is not what the specification says. We have just prototype constant folding. Isn't this a specific instance of constant folding? Because I see it as one. What am I missing?"
- 22:19 (L4833): "I disagree that coerce is running of arbitrary code. Coerce is just invocation of the numeric type constructor that gets the constants from the parser. That's all. It is just instantiation of the numeric types constructor using the values from the generic parameters of that coerce method. Invokes only constructor of the numeric type using the constants it has on hand. Like the type must provide a constructor that gets those parameters. That's it. That's the coercion."
- 22:21 (L4846): "That's what I had in my head. Does this match, can this be reconciled with what's written in the specification?"
- 22:33 (L4878): "Why do you keep talking about in literal and float literal when I said I will take the drafts originals? These two names, int literal and float literal, are from compiled library and from the glue classes in the walk interpreter. None of these were mentioned in the original specification, which defined the type for the natural numeral, radix numeral. We are going with those."
- 22:40 (L4903): "We'll go with machine defaults. When the type is not declared."
- 23:02 (L4982): "our coerce is a novel design, not this one. I basically said it will be a call. To initializer that must consume the fields from the numerals." He said this about the binary chapter's `where` arithmetic, which he declined to fulfil. His clarification on 11-09: he was explaining his understanding that the specification gives a custom type a way to read the original literal from the source by implementing the coercion; the coercion is not a run-time method call; it is the interface a custom numeric type implements, where the compiler has a chance to hand it the parameters from the source code.
- 23:10 (L5019): "Doesn't the natural numeral imply there is no sign, that it's only positive numbers, or am I mixing things up?"
- 11-09 13:20 (L6379): "I never gave up working draft static parameter form. Where do you get this?" 13:22 (L6388): "No fucking getters. Where wasn't I clear enough? I was talking about constant folding."

content.content:
We first define a notion of more specific types in the presence of coercion.
Recall from \secref{type-relations} that Fortress defines an
\emph{exclusion} relation between types which is denoted by $\excludes$.

For types $T$ and $U$, we say that $T$ \emph{rejects} $U$,
and write $T \rejects U$, if for all coercions to $T$, the type coerced
from excludes $U$:
\[
T \rejects U \iff \forall A: A \coercedefto T \implies A \excludes U.
\]
Note that $T \rejects U$ implies $U \not\coercesto T$.

We say that $T$ is \emph{no less specific} than $U$, and write $T
\morespecificeq U$, if $T$ is a subtype of $U$ or $T$ excludes, can be
coerced to, and rejects $U$:
\[
T \morespecificeq U \iff
T \Ovrsubtype U \logicor
(T \excludes U \logicand T \coercesto U \logicand T \rejects U).
\]

Recall from \secref{type-relations} that Fortress defines an

For types $T$ and $U$, we say that $T$ \emph{rejects} $U$,
and write $T \rejects U$, if for all coercions to $T$, the type coerced
from excludes $U$:
\[
T \rejects U \iff \forall A: A \coercedefto T \implies A \excludes U.
\]
Note that $T \rejects U$ implies $U \not\coercesto T$.

We say that $T$ is \emph{no less specific} than $U$, and write $T
\morespecificeq U$, if $T$ is a subtype of $U$ or $T$ excludes, can be
coerced to, and rejects $U$:
\[
T \morespecificeq U \iff
T \Ovrsubtype U \logicor
(T \excludes U \logicand T \coercesto U \logicand T \rejects U).
\]

- F-272 **The coercion example of the specification's "Coercion Resolution", over its own traits `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ128`, declares the exclusions that the chapter's definitions need: `ZZ32 excludes { ZZ64, ZZ128 }` and `ZZ64 excludes { ZZ128 }`.** A type `T` rejects `U` when every type that coerces to `T` excludes `U`. `T` is no less specific than `U` when it is a subtype of `U`, or excludes, coerces to and rejects it. So the choice of the more specific declaration depends on the exclusions. In the rung's probe, with the traits renamed `S32`, `S64` and `S128`, since the first two names are the library's, the revised example ran on both paths: `f(S32Of)`, on an `S32` value, chose `f` on `S64` and gave 1. No gated test runs the printed example. Row 394, fixed, names `tests/CoercionMostSpecificRungC.fss`, a walk test of the choice of the more specific coercion over three traits of the example's shape, each of which excludes both others. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md` section 4, decision 6; `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:521-537` (the definitions) and `:601` onward (the example).

\Library\ declare the two numeral types below the trait \TYP{Numeral}, which
extends \TYP{Number} and has no static parameters: \TYP{NaturalNumeral} below
\TYP{AnyNaturalNumeral} and \TYP{RadixPointNumeral} below
\TYP{AnyRadixPointNumeral}, two traits that extend \TYP{Numeral} and exclude
each other.
None of these traits declares a method.
\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

The radix of a numeral is ten, unless its digits are followed by an underscore
and a radix indicator (\secref{numerals}), which give its radix $r$; such a
numeral has one of the same two numeral types, with its radix as the static
argument $r$.
So \EXP{\mathtt{deadc}_{16}} has the type
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}5,16,912092\rrbracket}.

content.content:
## 3. Step 2: the one library

What was built (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, `.fss`; `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi`, `.fss`):

- The field numerals' two value objects, with their four getters, `asString`, `asFloat` and the 22 `=` pairs, are gone, with the two private helpers only `asString` used (`numeralDigits`, `numeralSuffix`). The `^` overloads on a numeral exponent (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`) are gone too: a numeral exponent converts at `^`'s other declarations.
- In their place, five traits with no members:

      trait Numeral extends Number end
      trait AnyNaturalNumeral extends Numeral excludes { AnyRadixPointNumeral } end
      trait AnyRadixPointNumeral extends Numeral end
      trait NaturalNumeral[\nat n, nat r, nat v\] extends AnyNaturalNumeral end
      trait RadixPointNumeral[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\] extends AnyRadixPointNumeral end

  The two `Any` traits exist only so that a type's coercion from each numeral type overloads with the other: two instantiations of different generic traits do not exclude each other otherwise. The library's own way for this is `AnyIntegral` above `Integral[\I\]`.
- Each of the eight number types takes a numeral by a coercion generic over the four numbers, whose body computes the value from them, as `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = v.asZZ32` at `ZZ32`, `= Ratio(v, 1)` and `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = v / r^(m.asZZ32)` at `QQ`, and `= numeralRR64(v, r.asZZ32, m.asZZ32)` at `RR64`, the library's one-rounding helper. `AnyIntegral`'s coercion chooses `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` from `v`.
- Lines: `git diff dd00743d9e --shortstat` over the four files: "4 files changed, 42 insertions(+), 145 deletions(-)".

content.content:
numerals, to the floating-point type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (the technical term for this kind of automatic
conversion is coercion); a value of any other integer type is converted to
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} explicitly (\secref{basic-rationals}).  In
this way one can write \EXP{(x + 1)/2} rather than \EXP{(x +
1.0)/2.0}, for example.  Such coercion applies generally to function
and method (collectively called as functional) calls as well as to
operators; one can write \EXP{\ln 2} rather than \EXP{\ln 2.0}, or
\EXP{\arctan(1,1)} rather than \EXP{\arctan(1.0,1.0)}, for example.
\revision{revival-int-float}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
Fortress supports the automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point
values.
The revival decided on 26~September 2026 that a conversion between number
types is a coercion where it is exact and stays explicit where it can lose
precision, and \library\ declare the coercion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} from
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and the decision names the integer numerals too.
The conversion from \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, though exact, stays explicit, since
that decision names only \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and the numerals.
The examples of this paragraph convert numerals and are unchanged.
\Library\ give an integer numeral a type
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}, from which
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} coerces by a coercion generic over the numeral's four
numbers, with one rounding; the compiled type checker,
against \library, and the interpreter convert an integer numeral where
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} is declared, whatever its value (\secref{literals},
\secref{revival-numerals}).
The compiled path's own library declares no coercion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
from an integer type or from \TYP{NaturalNumeral}; there \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and integer
numerals convert to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} only explicitly, and the other integer types not at all.}

One way to think about coercion is that if type \VAR{T} can be coerced
to type \VAR{U}, then a value of type \VAR{T} can be used to ``stand
in'' for a value of type \VAR{U} in a functional call, for example.  This is
different from actually \emph{being} of type \VAR{U}; it means only
that, given any value of type \VAR{T}, an appropriate value of type
\VAR{U} can be computed to substitute for it.  Also, coercion occurs
only when the declared type of the corresponding parameter in the
functional declaration is exactly the type \VAR{U} being coerced to
 not if it is a supertype of \VAR{U}.  Note, however, that if type
 \VAR{T} can be coerced to type \VAR{U} then any subtype of \VAR{T}
 can also be coerced to type \VAR{U}.

A numeral's conversion into its default (\secref{literals}) is not a coercion,
and applies where coercion does not: where the declared type is a supertype of
the default, as \TYP{Any}, \TYP{Object} and \TYP{Number} are, or is a type
parameter declared without a bound, and where no type is declared.
At a call, a numeral is applicable without coercion to a parameter of its
default type and to a parameter of a type that fixes no type for it; its
conversion into any other type is a coercion
(\secref{applicability-with-coercion}).
So of the declarations \EXP{h(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)} and
\EXP{h(x\COLON\TYP{Any})}, both applicable to \EXP{h(5)} without coercion, the
call invokes the first, which is the more specific.
A numeral at a type of a program's own that declares no coercion from the
numeral's type is not converted into its default and then coerced, since
coercion does not chain (below); it is a static error.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 made coercion
the only conversion of a value at a place of another type, and excluded a place
whose declared type is a supertype of the type converted to.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that a numeral where nothing fixes a
type is converted into its default; the default is a rule beside coercion, and
the paragraph above stands as it was.
It decided on 9~November 2026 that a numeral's coercion into a type is the one
that the type declares from the numeral's type, generic over the numeral's four
numbers (\secref{literals}), for the number types of \library\ as for a type of
a program's own.}

(* A numeral takes its default where nothing fixes a type, and converts from its exact value where a declared number type fixes one. *)
component NumeralTypesWalk
export Executable

kind(v: Any): String =
  typecase v of
    ZZ32 => "ZZ32"
    ZZ64 => "ZZ64"
    NN32 => "NN32"
    NN64 => "NN64"
    ZZ => "ZZ"
    QQ => "QQ"
    RR64 => "RR64"
    RR32 => "RR32"
    else => "another type"
  end

atAny(v: Any): String = kind(v)
atNumber(v: Number): String = kind(v)
second[\T\](a: T, b: T): T = b

run(): () = do
    x = 3
    assert(kind(x), "ZZ32", "x = 3 is a ZZ32")
    z: ZZ32 = 3
    assert(x SEQV z, "x = 3 is SEQV a ZZ32 3")
    y = 0.5
    assert(kind(y), "RR64", "y = 0.5 is an RR64")
    w: RR64 = 0.5
    assert(y SEQV w, "y = 0.5 is SEQV an RR64 0.5")
    bigN = 3000000000
    assert(kind(bigN), "ZZ64", "bigN = 3000000000 is a ZZ64")
    assert(atAny(3), "ZZ32", "3 at Any is a ZZ32")
    assert(atAny(0.5), "RR64", "0.5 at Any is an RR64")
    assert(atNumber(3), "ZZ32", "3 at Number is a ZZ32")
    assert(kind(second(13.0, 5)), "RR64", "second(13.0, 5) is at RR64")
    assert(second(13.0, 5) SEQV 5.0, "second(13.0, 5) is the RR64 5.0")
    assert(kind(second(0.5, 3000000000)), "RR64", "second(0.5, 3000000000) is at RR64")
    assert(second(0.5, 3000000000) SEQV 3000000000.0, "second(0.5, 3000000000) is the RR64 3000000000.0")
    assert(kind(second(1, 3000000000)), "ZZ64", "second(1, 3000000000) is at ZZ64")
    assert(1/2 = 0.5, "1/2 = 0.5 through QQ's = with the float numeral")
    assert(0.5 = 1/2, "0.5 = 1/2 through the reversed =")
    b = 0.9
    assert(kind(1 - b), "RR64", "1 - b is an RR64")
    assert(kind(b^2), "RR64", "b^2 is an RR64")
    s: ZZ32 = 4
    assert(kind(1.0 s), "RR64", "1.0 s is an RR64")
    assert((1.0 s) SEQV w 8, "1.0 s is the RR64 4.0")

    q: QQ = 0.1
    assert(numerator(q), 1, "q: QQ = 0.1 has numerator 1")
    assert(denominator(q), 10, "q: QQ = 0.1 has denominator 10")
    one: RR64 = w + w
    ten: RR64 = one + one + one + one + one + one + one + one + one + one
    r: RR64 = 0.1
    assert(r SEQV (one / ten), "r: RR64 = 0.1 is SEQV a computed RR64 0.1")
    t: RR64 = 0.77425264282026984
    assert(t.asString, "0.7742526428202698", "the numeral at RR64 rounds once")
    n: NN32 = 5
    assert(n, unsigned(5), "n: NN32 = 5")

content.content:
# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild

**tree**
: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.

**library order**
: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.

**DSL grammar**
: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.

**parser directory**
: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.

## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:

- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.

## Two layers of code

The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.

The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.

The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:

- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.

An edit makes stale what was built from it:

- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.

content.content:
Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect them to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it immediately to a floating-point number
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used in an expression
involving floating-point intervals,
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).


\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
is a static expression whose value is rational.
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.
